## Known risks and mitigations

The biggest risk is that the models are too honest: if envoys relay everything faithfully and leaders stay polite, the core mechanic goes flat. The milestones are built, but most risks below wait for the model games after the build order ("No model games until the build order is done" under Build order).

| Risk | Why it matters | Mitigation | Check at |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Envoys and leaders are too honest or cooperative | Language models lean toward helpfulness and honesty; without distortion and betrayal the game has no tension | Characters decide for themselves, informed by traits written into their persona as values and temptations, and script characters decide by formula from the same traits, so the two can be compared; if they prove too honest, the fix is real stakes and the facts to weigh them, never priming them to misbehave ("Stakes, not dispositions"). In the first agent simulation the Sonnet kings were not too honest: they sealed tablets they meant to break and planned betrayals in their journals; in the second, Haiku characters were honest, in games that barely tempted them and a world where gold was still worth little to them. For leaders: state plainly that breaking oaths, lying to rivals and bribing envoys are legitimate moves that every king knows the others may make, and keep the private journal as the place to plan a betrayal; a written strategy for each model king is only an idea for later ("A written strategy for model kings"). In AI Diplomacy (2025), deceptive models won while Claude often chose peace over victory | Model games after the build order |
| Mediated communication frustrates humans | Never saying exactly what you mean can feel like powerlessness, not intrigue | Feedback loops: spies that confirm or contradict, tablets as proof, envoy reputations players can learn over time | First mixed human and AI games |
| Cost per game is unknown | Decides whether bring-your-own-key and async play are viable | Measure tokens per seat, per turn and per game; show an estimate on the setup screen; prompt caching and message caps; calls spent where they matter most ("Minds follow what is at stake") | Model games after the build order |
| Leader memory grows without bound | Leaders hold the longest histories; cost rises and reasoning degrades. Confirmed in the first agent simulation: the agents' orders calls grew to about 50k tokens and four minutes each by season 5. Leader memory today covers about 13 seasons, against an average game of about 21 seasons today, and a median of 44 once item 6a's ending is built | A per-court ledger of promises, betrayals, tablets and payments, plus the last few turns verbatim; older turns summarized. Needed now that sieges have lengthened games | Build order item 6b |
| Turns are slow | Many sequential model calls per turn make play and batch runs drag | Run calls within a phase in parallel; audiences at different courts run concurrently; set a target time per turn | Model games after the build order |
| Success signals are hard to measure | Accusations, reputation and invented norms live in free text | Count engine events directly (tablets sealed, forgeries, assays); use a model as judge with a fixed rubric for the rest, checked against a hand-labeled sample | Before the ten-game experiment |
| Models replay real history | Models know the Amarna period and may follow it instead of playing to win | The primer experiment; leaders told their only goal is to win; compare games with and without historical framing | Primer experiment |
| Scope creep | The expansion list is long and every idea is tempting | Hold the prototype to its scope table; expansions start only after the success criteria are met | Every milestone |
